questions.q: What kind of course is Engineering 505 B, Chemistry?
options: A full semester of MIT chemistry
A Brief Foundations course in chemistry for Anderson Engineering: an overview and six lectures, about an hour
An optional elective outside the Foundations
questions.explain:
Paragraph 0.1: Paragraph 0.1 gives the format.
A is wrong: A Brief course is a first hour, not a substitute.
C is wrong: It is a Foundations course.
D is wrong: It is a lecture course.

questions.q: What background does the overview assume?
options: Logarithms, exponentials, and rates of change from Calculus One; no earlier chemistry course
questions.explain:
Paragraph 0.7: Some acquaintance with energy and force from Physics One also helps.
A is wrong: No earlier chemistry course is assumed.
B is wrong: It is not listed.
C is wrong: It is not required.

questions.q: Which MIT subjects form the backbone of this course?
options: 3.091 Introduction to Solid-State Chemistry and 5.111 Principles of Chemical Science
questions.explain:
Paragraph 0.9: The overview credits Professor Grossman (3.091) and Professor Drennan and Dr Vogel Taylor (5.111).
A is wrong: That is a mathematics subject.
C is wrong: That is a physics subject.
D is wrong: That is a biology subject.

questions.q: About how many particles are in one mole?
questions.explain:
Paragraph 1.2: One mole is about 6.02 × 10²³ particles.
B is wrong: The exponent is positive; a mole is an enormous number.
C is wrong: A mole is far larger than a thousand.
D is wrong: That is the Coulomb constant, not Avogadro's number.

questions.q: What did Rutherford's experiments around 1911 show?
options: Nearly all an atom's mass and positive charge sit in a tiny nucleus
Electrons orbit in fixed energy levels
questions.explain:
Paragraph 1.3: The nucleus is about a hundred thousand times smaller than the atom.
B is wrong: That was Bohr's 1913 proposal.
C is wrong: The experiments revealed internal structure.
D is wrong: That came later with quantum mechanics.

questions.q: In hydrogen, the drop from level three to level two emits light of about what wavelength?
options: About 656 nm, red light, from an energy gap of about 1.9 eV
questions.explain:
Paragraph 1.5: A fixed energy gap gives a fixed photon wavelength, λ = hc/ΔE.
A is wrong: That is the drop from level two to level one.
C is wrong: The energy gap is far too large for microwaves.
D is wrong: Hydrogen emits only sharp lines.

questions.q: What does the angular momentum quantum number l set?
options: The shape of the orbital, running from 0 to n − 1
The number of electrons in the atom
questions.explain:
Paragraph 1.7: l = 0, 1, 2, 3 correspond to s, p, d, f.
A is wrong: That is m_s.
B is wrong: That is n.
D is wrong: That is the atomic number.

questions.q: What does the Pauli exclusion principle imply for an orbital?
options: It holds at most eight electrons
It holds any number of electrons with the same spin
It must contain exactly one electron
It holds at most two electrons, with opposite spins
questions.explain:
Paragraph 1.8: No two electrons in an atom may share all four quantum numbers.
A is wrong: Eight is the capacity of an s plus p shell, not one orbital.
B is wrong: Same-spin electrons cannot share an orbital.
C is wrong: Orbitals may hold zero, one, or two.

questions.q: What is the electron configuration of sodium, with eleven electrons?
questions.explain:
Paragraph 1.9: Orbitals fill from the lowest energy upward by the aufbau principle.
B is wrong: A p subshell holds at most six electrons.
C is wrong: 3s fills before 3p.
D is wrong: An s subshell holds at most two electrons.

questions.q: Why do elements in the same group behave alike?
options: They have the same atomic mass
They have the same number of shells
They have the same number of neutrons
They have the same arrangement of valence electrons
questions.explain:
Paragraph 1.11: Valence electrons do nearly all of chemistry.
A is wrong: Masses differ widely down a group.
B is wrong: That is true of a period, not a group.
C is wrong: Neutrons do not set chemistry.

questions.q: How do atomic radius and ionisation energy vary across a period?
options: Radius increases and ionisation energy falls
Radius decreases and ionisation energy rises
questions.explain:
Paragraph 1.13: Effective nuclear charge rises across a period, pulling valence electrons in more tightly.
A is wrong: That is the trend down a group.
C is wrong: They move in opposite directions.
D is wrong: Both change smoothly across a period.

questions.q: How does an ionic bond form?
options: One atom transfers electrons to another and the ions attract electrostatically
Two atoms share an electron pair equally
Electrons spread over the whole solid
questions.explain:
Paragraph 2.2: Sodium gives its 3s electron to chlorine, and Na⁺ and Cl⁻ attract.
B is wrong: That is a covalent bond.
C is wrong: That is metallic bonding.
D is wrong: That is an intermolecular force.

questions.q: Why does magnesium oxide have a much larger lattice energy than sodium chloride?
options: Its ions carry charges of 2+ and 2− and are smaller, so the Coulomb attraction is much stronger
questions.explain:
Paragraph 2.3: Attraction grows with the product of ionic charges and falls with distance; MgO's lattice energy is nearly five times that of NaCl.
A is wrong: MgO is an ionic solid.
B is wrong: Smaller ions make the attraction stronger.
D is wrong: Its ions are Mg²⁺ and O²⁻.

questions.q: By VSEPR, what shape and angle do four electron domains with no lone pairs give, as in methane?
questions.explain:
Paragraph 2.7: Electron domains spread as far apart as possible.
A is wrong: Four domains spread further apart in three dimensions.
B is wrong: That is for three domains.
C is wrong: That is for two domains.

questions.q: Why is the H–O–H angle in water smaller than the tetrahedral angle?
options: Its two lone pairs take up more room than bonding pairs, squeezing the bonds together
Water has only two electron domains
questions.explain:
Paragraph 2.8: Water has four domains, two of them lone pairs, giving a bent shape near 104.5°.
B is wrong: It has two bonds and two lone pairs, four domains.
C is wrong: The cause is lone-pair repulsion.
D is wrong: Water is bent.

questions.q: Why is carbon dioxide non-polar although its C=O bonds are polar?
options: Carbon and oxygen have equal electronegativity
It has lone pairs on carbon
The molecule is linear, so the two bond dipoles cancel
questions.explain:
Paragraph 2.9: Overall polarity depends on both bond polarity and shape.
A is wrong: Oxygen is more electronegative, so the bonds are polar.
B is wrong: Carbon in CO₂ has no lone pairs.
C is wrong: CO₂ is covalent.

questions.q: What hybrid orbitals explain the tetrahedral geometry of methane?
options: Four sp³ hybrids from one 2s and three 2p orbitals
questions.explain:
Paragraph 2.10: They point to the corners of a tetrahedron.
A is wrong: sp gives a linear geometry.
B is wrong: sp² gives a trigonal planar geometry.
C is wrong: These would give 90° angles.

questions.q: What does molecular orbital theory explain about O₂ that simple Lewis structures miss?
options: O₂ has two unpaired electrons, so liquid oxygen is attracted to a magnet
questions.explain:
Paragraph 2.11: Filling bonding and antibonding molecular orbitals leaves two unpaired electrons.
A is wrong: Its bond order is two.
C is wrong: O₂ is a covalent molecule.
D is wrong: It has a bond order of two.

questions.q: What explains the electrical conductivity of metals?
options: Delocalised valence electrons shared by the whole solid
questions.explain:
Paragraph 2.12: The 'sea of electrons' moves freely around the ion lattice.
B is wrong: Lone pairs are localised.
C is wrong: Metal atoms are not ionically bonded to each other.
D is wrong: A wide gap makes an insulator.

questions.q: Which intermolecular force acts between all molecules and grows with molecular size?
questions.explain:
Paragraph 2.13: They arise from momentary fluctuations in electron clouds.
A is wrong: That needs H bonded to N, O, or F.
C is wrong: That is a bond within an ionic solid.
D is wrong: These act only between polar molecules.

questions.q: How many atoms does a face-centred cubic unit cell contain?
questions.explain:
Paragraph 3.4: Eight corners × 1/8 + six faces × 1/2 = 1 + 3 = 4.
B is wrong: That is body-centred cubic.
C is wrong: That is simple cubic.
D is wrong: Shared atoms count only in part.

questions.q: Which cubic arrangement has the highest packing efficiency?
questions.explain:
Paragraph 3.5: FCC, like hexagonal close packing, reaches the largest value possible for equal spheres.
A is wrong: Simple cubic is the least efficient.
B is wrong: BCC is between the two.
D is wrong: They differ markedly.

questions.q: What is the coordination number in an FCC metal?
questions.explain:
Paragraph 3.6: Each atom has twelve nearest neighbours in FCC and in hexagonal close packing.
A is wrong: That is simple cubic.
B is wrong: That is BCC.
D is wrong: That is far too few for a close-packed metal.

questions.q: How are the Miller indices of a plane found?
options: Take the intercepts in units of the cell edge, take reciprocals, and clear fractions
Measure the angle of the plane
Count the atoms on the plane
questions.explain:
Paragraph 3.7: A plane parallel to an axis has an infinite intercept and index zero.
A is wrong: The recipe uses reciprocals.
C is wrong: Indices come from intercepts.
D is wrong: That gives planar density, not indices.

questions.q: What does Bragg's law state?
questions.explain:
Paragraph 3.9: Waves reflected from successive planes add when the extra path, 2d sin θ, is a whole number of wavelengths.
A is wrong: The extra path is twice d sin θ, and n may be any whole number.
B is wrong: The path difference is proportional to sin θ.
D is wrong: θ is measured from the planes, giving sine.

questions.q: What is a vacancy in a crystal?
options: An extra atom between regular sites
A missing atom at a lattice site
questions.explain:
Paragraph 3.11: It is a point defect, and vacancies let atoms diffuse.
A is wrong: That is an interstitial.
B is wrong: That is a dislocation.
C is wrong: That is a planar defect.

questions.q: How do metals deform permanently?
options: By breaking all the bonds on a plane at once
By the movement of dislocations through the crystal
questions.explain:
Paragraph 3.12: Dislocations glide by breaking and remaking only a row of bonds at a time.
A is wrong: That would need far more force than is observed.
B is wrong: Plastic deformation is a slip process.
C is wrong: Boundaries obstruct dislocations; they do not melt.

questions.q: Why do smaller grains usually make a metal stronger?
options: More grain boundaries obstruct dislocation motion
questions.explain:
Paragraph 3.13: Boundaries are obstacles to the slip that causes permanent deformation.
A is wrong: Dislocations still exist.
B is wrong: They remain crystalline.
D is wrong: It has a strong effect.

questions.q: What does Hess's law say?
options: Enthalpy changes depend on the path
The enthalpy change of an overall reaction is the sum of the changes for steps that add up to it
Entropy always increases in a reaction
questions.explain:
Paragraph 4.3: Enthalpy is a state function.
A is wrong: As a state function, enthalpy does not.
B is wrong: Some, like dissolving ammonium nitrate, are endothermic.
D is wrong: That is not Hess's law.

questions.q: What is the standard enthalpy of formation of an element in its standard state?
questions.explain:
Paragraph 4.4: Formation enthalpies are measured relative to the elements in their standard states.
A is wrong: It is defined as zero.
C is wrong: Lattice energy is a different quantity.
D is wrong: It is zero by definition.

questions.q: What does the second law of thermodynamics say about a spontaneous process?
options: The total entropy of system plus surroundings increases
questions.explain:
Paragraph 4.6: Heat released raises the surroundings' entropy by q/T.
A is wrong: The total, not the system's alone, must increase.
B is wrong: Energy is conserved.
D is wrong: Endothermic processes can be spontaneous.

questions.q: When is a process at constant temperature and pressure spontaneous?
options: When ΔG = ΔH − TΔS is negative
questions.explain:
Paragraph 4.7: Negative ΔG means thermodynamically favoured, though not necessarily fast.
A is wrong: Ice melting is spontaneous though endothermic.
B is wrong: Negative entropy change works against spontaneity.
C is wrong: Positive ΔG means not spontaneous.

questions.q: Why does diamond not turn into graphite at room temperature although ΔG is negative?
options: Spontaneous means thermodynamically favoured, not fast; the change is immeasurably slow
Diamond is more stable than graphite
questions.explain:
Paragraph 4.7: Kinetics, not thermodynamics, sets the speed.
B is wrong: Graphite is the more stable form at room conditions.
C is wrong: The text states it is negative.
D is wrong: No; it is extremely slow.

questions.q: If ΔH is positive and ΔS positive, when is the process spontaneous?
questions.explain:
Paragraph 4.8: The −TΔS term must outweigh ΔH, which happens above a threshold temperature.
A is wrong: That is for negative ΔH and positive ΔS.
B is wrong: That is for positive ΔH and negative ΔS.
C is wrong: Low temperature favours negative ΔH with negative ΔS.

questions.q: What does ΔG° = −RT ln K imply for a reaction with negative ΔG°?
options: K is greater than one, so products are favoured
questions.explain:
Paragraph 4.11: At room temperature, each 5.7 kJ/mol change in ΔG° changes K tenfold.
B is wrong: That is for positive ΔG°.
C is wrong: K is always positive.
D is wrong: Thermodynamics says nothing about speed.

questions.q: By Le Chatelier's principle, what happens when a product is removed from an equilibrium mixture?
options: The reaction shifts forward to replace it
questions.explain:
Paragraph 4.13: The system shifts to partly counteract the disturbance.
A is wrong: Removing product favours the forward reaction.
C is wrong: Concentration changes do not change K.
D is wrong: The equilibrium shifts.

questions.q: What is K_w at 25 °C?
questions.explain:
Paragraph 5.2: It is the product of hydronium and hydroxide concentrations in water.
A is wrong: That is each ion's concentration in pure water.
C is wrong: That is pH + pOH.
D is wrong: That is the pH of pure water.

questions.q: How much more hydronium does a solution of pH 3 contain than one of pH 5?
questions.explain:
Paragraph 5.3: Each pH unit is a factor of ten, and two units is a factor of a hundred.
A is wrong: The scale is logarithmic.
B is wrong: Each unit is a factor of ten, not ten units.
D is wrong: Lower pH means more hydronium.

questions.q: What does a buffer contain?
options: A weak acid and its conjugate base in comparable amounts
A strong acid and a strong base in equal amounts
questions.explain:
Paragraph 5.5: Added acid is consumed by the base and added base by the acid, so pH changes little.
A is wrong: A strong acid cannot absorb added acid.
C is wrong: Water alone has no buffering capacity.
D is wrong: That just gives a neutral salt solution.

questions.q: What is oxidation?
questions.explain:
Paragraph 5.7: OIL RIG: oxidation is loss, reduction is gain.
A is wrong: That is reduction.
B is wrong: That is acid–base chemistry.
C is wrong: Oxidation is defined by electron transfer.

questions.q: What is the standard voltage of the Daniell cell, with E°(Cu²⁺/Cu) = +0.34 V and E°(Zn²⁺/Zn) = −0.76 V?
questions.explain:
Paragraph 5.10: E°cell = cathode − anode = 0.34 − (−0.76) = 1.10 V.
A is wrong: That subtracts the magnitudes instead of the signed potentials.
B is wrong: A spontaneous cell has a positive voltage.
D is wrong: That is not cathode minus anode.

questions.q: What is ΔG° for the Daniell cell, with n = 2 and E° = 1.10 V?
questions.explain:
Paragraph 5.11: ΔG° = −nFE° = −2 × 96,485 × 1.10 J/mol.
B is wrong: A positive voltage gives negative ΔG°.
C is wrong: Two electrons are transferred.
D is wrong: The Faraday constant is about 96,485 C/mol.

questions.q: What happens to a battery's voltage as Q approaches K, by the Nernst equation?
options: It falls to zero, and the battery is flat
questions.explain:
Paragraph 5.12: E = E° − (RT/nF) ln Q, and E = 0 when Q = K.
A is wrong: Products accumulate and the voltage falls.
B is wrong: E° holds only under standard conditions.
D is wrong: The voltage falls to zero at equilibrium.

questions.q: About what voltage does a lithium-ion cell provide?
questions.explain:
Paragraph 5.13: This high voltage is why it dominates phones and electric vehicles.
A is wrong: That is the Daniell cell.
B is wrong: That is a lead-acid cell.
D is wrong: That is a six-cell lead-acid battery.

questions.q: What is the half-life of a first-order reaction with rate constant k?
options: ln 2 / k, independent of the starting amount
It grows as the reaction proceeds
questions.explain:
Paragraph 6.2: Exponential decay halves in a fixed time, about 0.693/k.
B is wrong: That is the second-order half-life.
C is wrong: Half-life has units of time, inverse to k.
D is wrong: That describes second order.

questions.q: Near room temperature, roughly what does a 10 °C rise do to many reaction rates?
questions.explain:
Paragraph 6.5: The Arrhenius factor e^(−Ea/RT) is very sensitive to temperature.
B is wrong: Rates depend strongly on temperature.
C is wrong: Higher temperature raises rates.
D is wrong: The usual rule of thumb is about a factor of two.

questions.q: What does a catalyst change?
options: The activation energy, by providing a different pathway
questions.explain:
Paragraph 6.6: It speeds forward and reverse reactions alike and is not consumed.
A is wrong: A catalyst does not change K.
C is wrong: ΔG is unchanged.
D is wrong: Equilibrium composition is unchanged; it is reached faster.

questions.q: If atoms diffuse a certain depth in one hour, how long to diffuse twice as deep?
questions.explain:
Paragraph 6.9: Diffusion distance grows with √(Dt), so doubling depth takes four times as long.
A is wrong: Depth grows with the square root of time.
B is wrong: Deeper diffusion takes longer.
C is wrong: The relation is square, not cube.

questions.q: What holds polyethylene chains to one another?
options: Covalent bonds between every pair of chains
questions.explain:
Paragraph 6.12: Within a chain, covalent carbon–carbon bonds are strong.
B is wrong: Polyethylene is not a metal.
C is wrong: Polyethylene is not ionic.
D is wrong: Then it would not soften on heating.

questions.q: Why does a semiconductor's conductivity rise with temperature?
options: Its band gap is very wide
More electrons are thermally excited across its modest band gap
It has a partly filled band like a metal
questions.explain:
Paragraph 6.13: Silicon's gap is about 1.1 eV, small enough for some thermal excitation.
A is wrong: A wide gap is the mark of an insulator.
C is wrong: Metals' conductivity falls with temperature.
D is wrong: The key is carriers crossing the gap.
